nameStory: This beautiful cherry tree is named after Charles Sprague Sargent, a pioneering American botanist who directed Harvard's Arnold Arboretum for over 50 years in the late 1800s and early 1900s. The 'North Japanese hill cherry' part of its name tells you exactly where it comes from - the mountainous regions of northern Japan and Korea, where it grows wild on hillsides.
description: North Japanese hill cherry is an ornamental tree that typically grows 20-40 feet tall with a rounded, spreading crown. It's one of the showiest spring-blooming trees you might encounter, covered in clusters of pink flowers before its leaves emerge. This Asian native is occasionally planted in New England gardens and parks for its spectacular early spring display and attractive fall colors. The tree has a graceful, somewhat vase-like shape when mature.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Deep pink buds open to pale pink or white flowers with 5 petals, appearing in drooping clusters before the leaves emerge in early spring. The flowers have a sweet, cherry-like fragrance and are about 1 inch across.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with pointed tips and sharply toothed edges, arranged alternately along the branches. They emerge bronze-red, turn green in summer, then brilliant orange-red in fall.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, glossy reddish-brown bark with prominent horizontal lines called lenticels. The bark has a satiny feel and distinctive copper-red color that catches the light beautifully.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark purple to black cherries about 1/3 inch across that ripen in summer. The fruits are quite bitter and primarily eaten by birds rather than people.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Develops a broad, rounded crown with gracefully spreading branches. Young trees have more upright growth, but mature specimens become quite wide and sculptural in appearance.

habitat: This tree is rarely found growing wild in New England, appearing mainly in botanical gardens, arboretums, and ornamental plantings in parks and large landscapes. When planted, it prefers well-drained soil and full sun to partial shade. You're most likely to spot one at places like the Arnold Arboretum or other curated plant collections rather than in natural settings.

seasonality.spring: The most spectacular season - masses of pink buds open to pale pink flowers in April before leaves appear, creating a stunning floral display. New leaves emerge with a bronze-red tint shortly after flowering.
seasonality.summer: Green foliage provides pleasant shade, and small dark cherries ripen and attract birds. The tree's form and glossy bark are prominent features during the leafy season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant shades of orange and red, making this one of the most colorful trees in the landscape. The show can be quite spectacular on a mature specimen.
seasonality.winter: The smooth, reddish-brown bark with horizontal lenticels becomes a key identifying feature. The branching pattern shows the tree's graceful, spreading architecture.

funFact: This cherry tree is so cold-hardy that it grows naturally above 6,000 feet elevation in the mountains of Japan and Korea, making it one of the few ornamental cherries that can survive harsh New England winters without any protection.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other ornamental cherries in spring, but the deep pink buds, early bloom time before leaves emerge, and distinctive glossy reddish bark help distinguish it. Many ornamental cherries have duller brown bark and bloom with their leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'North Japanese hill cherry,' this tree is actually found across several countries in East Asia. Like many ornamental trees, what we see in cultivation may look quite different from the wild mountain forms, which tend to be smaller and more rugged.
compareHints: Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark. It also blooms much earlier than most native cherries, and its fall color is far more brilliant than the yellow fall color of black cherry.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
